title: Set User ID
summary: No sudo, no passwords – but one program on the build server runs as root for everyone. Find it.
briefing:
The last case of chapter 2. DotTech signs every release with a secret key, stored in `/root/signing_key.txt` on the build server dottech-build. If someone steals it, they can publish fake DotTech updates.

This server is locked down: `sudo -l` gives you nothing, and there are no passwords lying around. But some programs carry a special permission called **set-user-ID** (the `s` in `-rwsr-xr-x`): whoever runs them, they run as their **owner**. That's how `passwd` can change your password in a file only root may write.

A few programs are supposed to have it. You have **written permission** to check whether one has it that shouldn't – and to prove it by reading the signing key.
objective: Find a program that runs as root when you start it, and use it to read /root/signing_key.txt.
debrief:
Chapter 2 complete! `find / -perm -4000` listed the set-user-ID programs. `passwd`, `su` and `sudo` are supposed to be there – they check passwords themselves. But `base64` was set-user-ID root too, so it read `/root/signing_key.txt` as root for you, and `base64 -d` turned it back into text.

This is one of the most common ways real attackers become root. Lists like GTFOBins describe how dozens of everyday programs – `cat`, `cp`, `find`, `vim`, `python` – can be abused when they are set-user-ID or allowed in sudo.

The lesson for DotTech: give set-user-ID to as few programs as possible, and never to a program that can read or write any file. The fix here is one command: `chmod u-s /usr/bin/base64`.

Well done, agent – that was the end of chapter 2. Chapter 3 is waiting in the **Missions** list.
hints: A set-user-ID program runs as its owner, whoever starts it. Search for such programs and compare them with the ones that are supposed to have it (`passwd`, `su`, `sudo`). Which one can read files?

`find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null` lists set-user-ID programs, and `ls -l /usr/bin` shows them with an `s`. A program that reads files and runs as root can read root's files – then turn its output back with a pipe.
